notes.title: Topic 10 - Bosses
notes.notes:
Conquering worlds in our game won’t always be easy, as defenders have their secret weapon! Each enemy faction will have special bosses they can summon for help. Every tenth enemy wave will spawn a boss from that faction, who will march down the longest path on the map, always marked by a glowing soul symbol at the portal. However, defeating a boss won’t be straightforward. Not only will bosses have much larger health pools than regular enemies, but they’ll also possess unique abilities that can significantly complicate both their defeat and the incoming wave of enemies. Additionally, if the player allows the boss to reach the Monolith, the invasion will end in failure, regardless of how healthy the Monolith was beforehand. So, be sure to fortify your defenses well before the 10th, 20th, and 30th rounds! 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/6a98f625c867dd68db419e5915fe5e5fd4cd99ef.jpg[/img]
A boss isn’t just a challenge for the player but also an opportunity, as defeating the first two bosses rewards the player with an additional upgrade. They’ll be able to choose this upgrade from a special pool of upgrades outside their regular deck. In this pool, most cards enhance all towers owned by the player. These upgrades may be necessary, as each subsequent boss will grow stronger! Defeating a boss is not only crucial for that specific game run but also for progression, as boss rounds mark milestones that significantly boost the amount of experience gained.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/c3094291c01208a9bf9aa6a4fe9abf9e322e02a3.jpg[/img]
To help players prepare for such an encounter, they will receive information before the game begins, detailing the boss’s elemental affinity and abilities. This allows the player to tailor their deck with cards that might be useful for facing such a formidable opponent.
—

notes.title: Topic 9 - Art Direction
notes.notes:
From the very start, the visual presentation of our game has been a priority for us. As a small two-person team with roots in graphic design, we’ve always valued the importance of strong visuals in game development. We wanted to create a visual style that would give us artistic freedom but wouldn't be too time-consuming to produce. After several visual experiments, we decided on a style that falls somewhere between stylized art and low poly. With the addition of shaders, lighting, and procedural terrain generation, we managed to achieve a look that satisfies us and still allows us to finish the game within the planned timeline. But that was just the first decision we had to make. Once we knew how we were going to create our models, we had to decide on the atmosphere and tone of the game.

We noticed that many similar games feature bright and saturated colors, but that didn’t quite fit our setting, where the player takes on the role of the villain. Plus, we wanted to stand out not just through visual quality, but also in terms of mood. So, we opted for something more mysterious. Low-saturation colors, eerie dark waves in the background, and thick fog that occasionally blankets the map. This is the aesthetic we’ve committed to, and it’s what you can see in our game right now.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/0939cd58a4e5e815b7ba70e00b2dc21c144a4f2d.jpg[/img]
At this point, we’ve focused on creating a world that isn’t too abstract—it somewhat resembles Earth, with green hills and trees. But nothing stops us from introducing completely different worlds in future updates. A world made entirely of crystals? Fiery plains on a planet straight out of hell? Or maybe a tropical world with colors nothing like what we’d expect on Earth? What do you think the next type of world Monolith will attack should look like?

By then, we knew how the world of our game would look, but we still hadn’t decided on the appearance of the creatures inhabiting it. Initially, we leaned toward classic monsters—skeletons and other fearsome-looking enemies. But something felt off; fighting them made us feel like we were the "good guys." So, we went back to the drawing board, looking for different inspiration, and we remembered games like Dungeon Keeper. Despite playing as the villain, not everything in that game is scary or intimidating—there’s a certain amount of quirkiness. After a few tests, we decided that the enemies in our game don’t need to look menacing. On the contrary, they can look like poor, innocent creatures—the kind Monolith would destroy with pleasure. And that’s how we created our first enemy. You’ve already seen it: it’s the Pebble Golem.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/0ca8b0d8c35b66d547029bbb1489d79c768e6796.jpg[/img]
—

notes.title: Topic 8 - Upgrade Deck
notes.notes:
During gameplay, upgrade cards are drawn randomly from the deck. The player can choose one of four drawn cards, with the rest going into a discard pile. At any point, the player can spend some souls to reshuffle all discarded cards back into the deck. Otherwise, this happens automatically when the deck runs out of cards. This system makes it easier for players to find specific cards, as unwanted cards are temporarily set aside, reducing the pool of available cards and increasing the chances of drawing the desired upgrade. We’re also considering adding other options where, for a price in souls, the player could discard the drawn upgrades and pull new ones.

We’re excited for you to try it out and share your feedback on these systems, and we look forward to hearing your suggestions on how we can further improve them!

—

notes.title: Topic 7 - Story
notes.notes:
Wandering Monolith is a game primarily focused on gameplay, but that doesn't mean we've completely forgotten about the lore of the world we're creating. From the beginning, we knew we wanted the player to take on the role of the antagonist. We also wanted to integrate gameplay elements with the lore so that both aspects form a cohesive whole. And thus, the titular Monolith was born.

The Monolith exists somewhere between a living and non-living entity; it serves as a catalyst for negative forces and energies. Using its powers, it can materialize towers that represent these energies and help fend off the resistance of the defenders of the worlds it invades. When the Monolith targets a world, its defenders have only 30 days to repel the invasion. If they succeed, the Monolith will leave their world, at least temporarily. However, if they fail, the life force of their world will be drained, and the world itself will be destroyed in the process. With each new world, the Monolith grows stronger, but the desperate defenders will put up even fiercer resistance. Wandering through time and space, the Monolith can strike at any moment, and all living beings must remain vigilant—no place in the cosmos is truly safe.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/74307b7fb67b3603645b2ed59806ae3cbe4a0db8.png[/img]
One aspect we wanted to develop in our game was the combat system. We decided to create interactions similar to the "rock, paper, scissors" mechanic—based on elements. Initially, we considered using classic elements like water, fire, etc. Ultimately, inspired by cosmic horror, we decided to use the energies that govern this universe, energies from which the Monolith itself is composed. The neutral element in our game is Corporeal, which represents the tangible aspects of the world—their fragility, commonality, and universality. The remaining elements form a ring of interactions, where each element has one weakness relative to another. The elemental interactions are as follows: Void -> Celestial -> Spectral -> Oblivion -> Abyss -> Void.

[i]The emptiness of the void eclipses and diminishes the brilliance of celestial energies.
The radiant power of celestial forces disperses and reveals the nature of spectral entities.
The elusive and intangible spectral entities navigate and elude the grasp of oblivion.
The concept of oblivion gradually consumes and diminishes the depths of the abyss.
The consuming darkness of the abyss absorbs and nullifies the emptiness of the void.[/i]

Although we could have easily leaned toward a sci-fi setting, we decided to maintain a dark fantasy and cosmic horror theme. You won’t encounter modern technology in our game, but you will find vast amounts of magic, ancient structures, and strange creatures like golems and shadows that inhabit countless worlds.

Through the lexicon included in the game, you’ll be able to learn more about the world you're destroying, thanks to the descriptions of the enemies you encounter.
---

notes.title: Topic 6 - Neutral structures
notes.notes:
The towers summoned by the player aren’t the only structures you’ll encounter during the game. During map generation, neutral structures can also appear, adding extra variety to the gameplay. At first glance, these might seem like they’re just filling space on the map, but we plan for each neutral structure to have its own unique function. As the game progresses, the player will unlock more of these structures, and they will appear in future runs.

One such structure already in the game is the Soulstone. Its primary function is to grant the player additional souls, which can later be spent on new towers. To activate the Soulstone, the player simply needs to build a tower next to it. For each tower built near a Soulstone, the player will receive bonus souls at the end of the round. Additionally, there are upgrade cards that enhance towers built next to the Soulstone, allowing them to deal extra damage to enemies.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/84bd62ea784cdb9cec626a2da1eb6de3ea8945d4.jpg[/img]
The cards a player includes in their deck can turn seemingly useless structures into valuable assets. For example, trees that might normally occupy map space can become useful. Soul Lantern has a card that transforms each tree near the tower into a haunted tree, which will attack enemies. As the game develops and more towers and cards are added, neutral structures will gain even more potential uses. Not to mention, some enemy abilities will also be able to interact with these structures.

Neutral structures offer another layer of strategy, allowing us to create interesting scenarios and encouraging players to test new tactics. If you could add a new neutral structure to the game, what would it be?

---

notes.title: Topic 5 - Upgrades
notes.notes:
Upgrade cards are a crucial element of our game – they can ultimately decide the outcome of a match. The cards included in your deck and the order in which they are chosen will have a significant impact on whether the run ends in success or failure.

Upgrade cards are divided into 3 tiers: common, uncommon, and rare. This division is based not only on the strength of their effects but also on how they influence the game. First-tier cards are the simplest – they generally provide a small benefit or a larger one at the cost of another stat. These upgrades focus on the core attributes of a tower. Their power isn’t too high because you can include up to three of the same card from this tier in your deck, allowing you to increase their effectiveness. These cards are designed so that even if a player picks opposing upgrades (e.g., increasing attack speed at the cost of damage and increasing damage at the cost of attack speed), the player will still come out slightly ahead. This allows for strategies that focus on one stat early in the game and then transition to another.

Uncommon and rare cards can only be added to your deck as a single copy. Second-tier cards typically offer bigger benefits but require meeting certain conditions to activate them, such as having the tower built near another tower. Since you can only have one copy in your deck, the effects of these cards are often more noticeable and can have a more dramatic impact. Upgrades in this tier can change how a tower is used, such as halving its range but doubling its damage.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/e1618b913e42147cf1534f610c290476a1d5ba74.jpg[/img]
Rare cards have the most dramatic effects and can sometimes completely change how a tower functions. They are often just very strong upgrades, such as doubling the range bonus for height placement, but they can also provide large bonuses with strict conditions, like only allowing one copy of the tower. In extreme cases, they might cause the tower to stop dealing damage but, for example, increase the rewards earned from killing enemies.

The design of these cards means that the best deck isn’t simply one filled with second- and third-tier cards but a well-balanced mix of upgrade cards from all tiers that work together and support the same strategy.

At the start of the game, players will only have access to some of the cards, and over time they will unlock more advanced ones. The player will decide in which order they are unlocked. We hope this will help players get familiar with the available options and avoid overwhelming them with too many choices at the beginning of the game.
---

notes.title: Topic 4 - Towers
notes.notes:
It wouldn’t be a tower defense game if the Monolith couldn’t summon towers. As mentioned earlier, there are five different elements in the game: Void, Celestial, Spectral, Oblivion, Abyss, and one neutral element - Corporeal. Each tower in the game will be associated with one of these elements. This means that its primary attack uses that element, but through upgrades and various cards, it may be possible to change the type of damage the tower deals.

Towers differ not only in their element but also in the way they attack. Some shoot at a single enemy, others deal area damage, and some shoot lasers that deal damage to all enemies in their path. Certain projectiles will explode, dealing additional damage, while others will slow down enemies or inflict damage over time (DoT). As the game progresses, you can expect more new and unique towers, each with its own set of upgrade cards.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/9072a9e196afeb8daced6eccb149ba0f604a5a96.jpg[/img]
In the upcoming demo, you will be able to test three of the planned towers. The first is the Shard Tower, a Corporeal tower that specializes in rapid attacks, firing multiple projectiles, and the ability to target more than one enemy at a time. Of course, which of these abilities gets enhanced will depend on the upgrades you choose during the game.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/d4fd663a3d8c77ddeda9770e6d6b8fad03319e6b.jpg[/img]
The next tower is the Soul Lantern, a Spectral tower. Its specialty is applying DoT effects to enemies. It has the potential to deal significant damage, provided that the enemy doesn’t get too close to the Monolith.

The final tower available in the demo is the Oblivion Hourglass, which specializes in slowing down enemies around it, but it can also be repurposed to deal damage.
---
We’re curious to see which of these towers you’ll like the most. At the start of early access, you can expect at least one tower from each element and unique upgrades for each of them, which you will be able to unlock during the game to build your own upgrade decks.

notes.title: Topic 3 - Enemies
notes.notes:
Last time, we discussed how the map is generated, and this topic is closely tied to the systems related to enemies. Each path in the game consists of several connected points. When a new map segment appears, its starting path point connects to the endpoint of the previous segment. At the beginning of each round, the game identifies all points that don’t have a subsequent connection and treats them as enemy spawn points. These points are marked with portals.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/269a91e66fc69a3648a265d60e013478a9de76c2.png[/img]

The enemy system has a "budget" that it can use to spawn enemies from the available pool. This budget increases with each round but also scales up with each additional fork in the map to maintain a consistent level of challenge when enemies are spread across multiple entrances. The game then spawns various enemies using the budget and distributes them evenly among all portals. As the game progresses, the enemy system can spawn more enemies and gains access to stronger variants. Similarly, every ten rounds, the game spawns a boss that must be defeated - otherwise, the run will end in failure.

Before the game starts, players are informed about the types of enemies and bosses they may encounter. Depending on the difficulty level chosen, they may face enemies from one or multiple elements in the game. Additionally, enemies are divided into different "families" each with its own unique characteristics and abilities. Currently, the planned families include golems, shadows, and blobs. Each of these families has units representing different elements - some may have variants for multiple elements, while others are tied to a single one. Before the game begins, an enemy family, element types, and a few enemy units fitting those criteria are selected for that map. This variety should encourage players to experiment with different strategies in each playthrough.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/791d3397b18ff1fe8e0f4583e35bc7e58f37d2c5.png[/img]
---
What other enemy families do you think should appear in our game?

If there are any topics you’d like to hear more about, feel free to let us know here or on our [url=https://discord.com/invite/DJWQq7zvpG]Discord[/url], where you can also find more of this devlogs sooner!

notes.title: Topic 2 - Map Generation
notes.notes:
Map generation was the first major task we tackled during the production of our game. We wanted the map to change between playthroughs, and for the player to have some influence over how their world evolves. Additionally, we wanted even segments with the same path to feel unique, through variations in the height of individual blocks and the presence of neutral buildings.

At that time, we heard a lot about different versions of the [i]Wave Function Collapse [/i]algorithm (there are tons of interesting YouTube videos on the subject - we highly recommend them!) and wanted to create something similar. However, after some analysis, we realized that for our needs, we could achieve similar results by using a simplified method inspired by that algorithm.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/9565d29dc324ccf6aaab28dffd99a1f63466c4dc.png[/img]
Ultimately, the map is generated from hand-crafted blocks (8x8) with different road shapes, on which we then apply additional variety. Since each map segment consists of smaller elements, their heights can be randomized according to set rules, as can some visual elements. Once the heights are determined, the game looks at the rule set for that map and generates neutral elements for the segment, such as trees and neutral buildings. When everything is in place, the segment is spawned underwater, and a sequence triggers, raising the entire block. Once all elements are positioned, the entire segment is merged into a single model.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45002947/2c09e8c75364a92778d77e4a49a8c19f2694ebc9.png[/img]

Where the road ends, a space appears where the next block can be generated. The decision of what segment comes next is made in real-time. The game checks which segments are already on the map and which potential segments could be placed there in the near future, then selects the one that best fits the current layout. This prevents situations where two roads would want to continue in the same spot, leading to loops with no start or end. Potential dead ends are blocked with segments containing portals, but the algorithm ensures that at least one path remains open until the final round is reached. Similarly, as the game nears its end, every open path will be closed with a portal segment.

This system is flexible enough that, in the future, it will allow us to create different rules and segment sets to further diversify the worlds we will be conquering!
---

notes.title: Topic 1 - The Idea Behind the Game
notes.notes:
We know it’s been a bit quiet here so far, but we want to change that. That’s why we’ve decided to start posting regular updates here to keep you informed about the progress of our game development. We’ll begin by sharing how our journey in game production started and gradually dive into more technical topics and plans for the future. 

As aspiring game developers, we had many ideas, but we knew we didn’t want to start with a massive project that could take ages to finish - if it ever did. We wanted to see how well we worked together, what we were capable of, and create something modern, with strategic decision-making and a visually appealing experience. That’s how the idea for a Tower Defense game with Deck Building elements came to be, initially called Project Monolith. It has since evolved into Wandering Monolith: Rogue TD, but let’s start from the beginning.

Wandering Monolith: Rogue TD, the game we’ll be discussing here, is born out of our fascination with Tower Defense games. The main inspirations are Rogue Tower and Plants vs. Zombies (see if you can guess which mechanics are inspired by which game!).

To deepen the combat system, we introduced different attack and armor types, interacting in a rock-paper-scissors style - in our game, these are Void, Celestial, Spectral, Oblivion, and Abyss. Before each run, players are informed of the types of enemies and armor they will face. Based on this, they must decide which towers to use and which upgrades to include in their deck.

These upgrades won’t just increase stats, like attack +1. Some will completely change how a tower is used. Players will unlock new upgrade cards between runs and create their own decks for future playthroughs.

With procedurally generated maps in real-time, this creates countless scenarios where players must show their strategic planning skills.

Though gameplay is the focus, we wanted to include a story as well. Without giving away too much, one key element is that the Monolith - the player - is actually the aggressor, invading a world, while hordes of enemies defend against the onslaught.
---
We hope this small introduction gives you a good idea of what our game is about.
